primary_cause: Broad industrial and recession repricing. No major negative 3M-specific news. Becoming central PPE supplier — later said would double N95 output to 1.1B units
secondary_factors: Global manufacturing and supply-chain disruption. Liquidation selling in cyclicals. Industrial cyclicality overwhelming PPE upside
store_description: 3M looked defensive because of masks but on March 16 investors were still treating it mainly as a global industrial exposed to factory shutdowns and recession risk. No material company-specific negative catalyst within the prior 72 hours.

primary_cause: Fear away-from-home consumption would slump as restaurants bars stadiums and events shut down. No major PepsiCo-specific negative
secondary_factors: General staples de-risking and marketwide forced selling. OpenTable data: Washington DC restaurant visits down 77% YoY on Mar 16. Restaurant traffic collapsing
store_description: PepsiCo had grocery exposure but investors were quickly discounting damage to foodservice convenience and impulse channels as public gathering restrictions spread. No company-specific negative announcement in the prior 72 hours.

primary_cause: Despite panic-buying investors worried higher labor sanitation stockout and supply-chain costs would offset revenue benefits. Reuters later showed foot traffic rose ~18% Mar 13-17
secondary_factors: Liquidation selling. Fear of broad consumer disruption. Walmart had announced coronavirus-related operating changes Mar 10. Not yet settled on stay-at-home winner narrative
store_description: Walmart was not being sold because demand disappeared. It was sold because March 16 was a balance-sheet and margin panic and investors feared that extraordinary traffic cleaning staffing and replenishment pressure would compress margins even as sales volumes spiked.

primary_cause: No material Pfizer-specific negative. Vaccine story not yet stock driver in mid-March 2020. Marketwide risk-off in pharma and healthcare
secondary_factors: Uncertainty around drug demand mix. Trial disruption risk. Portfolio de-risking
store_description: On March 16 Pfizer was still trading mostly as a large pharma defensive but even defensives were being sold in the forced liquidation. No meaningful company-specific bad news inside the prior 72 hours.

primary_cause: Shutdown risk to away-from-home beverage consumption. Reuters later noted venues representing about 50% of Coca-Cola revenue vulnerable to closure. No fresh KO-specific negative
secondary_factors: Event cancellations. Restaurant closures. General market liquidation
store_description: Unlike some staples Coke had substantial exposure to restaurants cinemas stadiums and fountain channels that suddenly looked impaired as gatherings were curtailed. No company-specific release in the previous 72 hours but the business-model exposure was obvious.

primary_cause: Banking-sector repricing after Fed cut rates to 0-0.25% on Mar 15 crushing NIM expectations. Largest U.S. banks including Wells said Mar 15 would stop buying back stock
secondary_factors: Buyback suspension. Recession and loss fears. Wells existing regulatory overhang and asset cap. Zero-rate policy looming credit losses
store_description: Wells was hit by a brutal combination: zero-rate policy looming credit losses and the March 15 buyback halt. For a bank already constrained by its asset cap and structurally weaker than peers the market read the emergency policy response as especially damaging to profitability and capital returns.

primary_cause: Store closures and concern device upgrades and retail activations would slow. Reuters Mar 14 reported Verizon temporarily closing a number of U.S. stores
secondary_factors: General market selloff. Concern over consumer and payment delinquencies. Relatively defensive which explains smaller decline
store_description: Verizon was relatively defensive which likely explains why it fell less than many cyclical names. Still with some stores shutting and the economy abruptly locking down investors started pricing in weaker equipment sales and lower retail activity.

primary_cause: Sudden collapse in travel and discretionary spend expectations. Reuters later said transaction volumes deteriorated rapidly especially cross-border travel-related spending
secondary_factors: Recession fears. Cross-border mix vulnerability. Domestic categories like travel restaurants entertainment and fuel also falling sharply. No Visa press release in prior 3 days
store_description: Visa's March 16 decline fits the market's realization that shutdowns would hammer its highest-margin cross-border business. Even without a fresh company filing the combination of travel bans gathering restrictions and collapsing restaurant and entertainment activity made Visa's earnings exposure unusually clear.

primary_cause: Zero-rate shock from Fed Mar 15 move. U.S. Bancorp announced Mar 15 would temporarily suspend share buyback for rest of Q1 and Q2 2020
secondary_factors: Rising recession and credit-loss fears. Same combination as money-center banks: collapse in NIM expectations anticipated credit stress and explicit suspension of capital returns
store_description: USB was viewed as a high-quality regional bank but quality did not matter much on March 16. The stock was repriced lower on the same combination as the money-center banks: a collapse in NIM expectations anticipated credit stress and explicit suspension of capital returns.

primary_cause: Concern over global trade B2B shipping and air-freight network disruption. Growing disruption in air and maritime freight canceled sailings collapsing passenger flights
secondary_factors: Recession fears. Uncertainty over delivery mix and costs. Too early for market to fully credit e-commerce offset. No UPS-specific negative announcement
store_description: March 16 was too early for the market to fully credit the e-commerce offset that later benefited parcel carriers. Instead investors focused on falling global trade travel restrictions and the risk that a deep recession would hit premium shipping and business volumes.

primary_cause: Expectation of sharp decline in industrial and intermodal rail volumes. Reuters: Port of Long Beach saw imports down 17.9% in February from COVID factory closures and canceled sailings
secondary_factors: Recession fears. Supply-chain disruptions. Exposure to trade-sensitive freight. No material UNP-specific announcement
store_description: Union Pacific was hit as investors extrapolated shrinking imports weaker industrial production and lower intermodal activity. No fresh UNP-specific negative headline inside the prior 72 hours so the stock move appears mainly driven by the fast-deteriorating freight outlook.

primary_cause: Investor fear COVID treatment costs would surge across managed care. Surgeon General urged hospitals Mar 14 to stop elective surgeries. Kaiser Permanente Mar 16 postponed elective and non-urgent procedures
secondary_factors: Confusion around elective-procedure economics. Policy risk. Forced selling. In hindsight deferred elective care helped insurers but market had not sorted that out yet on Mar 16
store_description: In hindsight deferred elective care helped insurers but on March 16 the market had not sorted that out yet. Investors saw a coming wave of medical claims utilization uncertainty and systemic healthcare stress which explains why UNH sold off far more violently than its later fundamentals justified.

primary_cause: Expected collapse in urban mobility airport trips and nightlife-related demand. Environment for ride-hailing deteriorating rapidly. United said Mar 16 would cut April-May capacity ~50%
secondary_factors: Profitability concerns. Funding-risk fears. General tech and high-beta deleveraging. No Uber-specific filing in prior 3 days but business-model exposure direct and severe
store_description: Uber was sold as investors realized stay-at-home behavior and travel shutdowns would hit the core rides business immediately. No major Uber-specific announcement in the prior 72 hours but the business-model exposure was direct and severe enough to explain the drop.

primary_cause: Semiconductor and industrial-demand repricing tied to recession and manufacturing shutdown fears. No TXN-specific negative headline
secondary_factors: Supply-chain disruption. Exposure to auto and industrial customers. Broad analog exposure to cyclical end markets especially industrial and automotive
store_description: Texas Instruments had broad analog exposure to cyclical end markets especially industrial and automotive both of which looked suddenly vulnerable on March 16. With no fresh company-specific catalyst found the move is best explained by a sharp downgrade to cyclical chip demand.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Reuters Mar 16 reported Exxon pledged significant spending cuts as crude collapsed. U.S. crude settled below $29 vs $61 at start of year. Shares touched levels last seen in 2003. Dividend yield hit record 10.1%
secondary_factors: Oil-price collapse plus pandemic demand shock. Capex cuts. Looming oversupply. Concern dividend might become stressed
store_description: This one had a real stock-specific headline. Exxon was already under pressure from the Saudi-Russia oil war and March 16 brought confirmation that management would cut spending hard because crude had cratered reinforcing fears about earnings cash flow and the sustainability of the dividend.

primary_cause: No formal Tesla shutdown announcement in prior 3 days. High-beta unwind plus fear sole major U.S. factory would be disrupted by Bay Area lockdowns
secondary_factors: Valuation compression. CEO messaging risk (Musk tweeted coronavirus panic was dumb). Recession fears hitting auto demand. Fremont about to come under lockdown pressure
store_description: Tesla's drop was larger than the market because it was one of the most crowded high-beta names and because production in Fremont was about to come under lockdown pressure. No clean negative company filing in the preceding 72 hours but the stock was extremely exposed.

primary_cause: No material negative TMO-specific item. Commercial COVID testing becoming future positive — later aimed for ~5M tests per week by April. Indiscriminate liquidation in life sciences and healthcare tools
secondary_factors: Concern about lab shutdowns research disruption and general market stress. Probably fell less because investors could already see testing upside
store_description: Thermo Fisher probably fell less because investors could already see testing upside. Still on March 16 the market was selling almost everything and there was no clearly negative company-specific headline to explain the move beyond broad liquidation.

primary_cause: No AT&T-specific negative. Marketwide de-risking plus concern about retail wireless activity and media and advertising exposure
secondary_factors: Debt leverage. Future WarnerMedia and theater disruption risk. Traded more like a leveraged defensive on March 16
store_description: AT&T traded more like a leveraged defensive on March 16 so it still got hit despite relatively resilient telecom service revenue. No fresh AT&T-specific negative catalyst in the prior 72 hours.

primary_cause: Investors pricing catastrophic cash-flow loss for enclosed malls and retail rents. Reuters Mar 18 reported Simon would close all U.S. malls and outlets until Mar 29. By Mar 16 CDC guidance and expanding shutdown orders already making mall traffic impairment obvious
secondary_factors: Tenant distress. Dividend fears. REIT balance-sheet concerns. One of clearest business-model selloffs of the day
store_description: SPG's plunge was one of the clearest business-model selloffs of the day. Even before the formal March 18 closure announcement the combination of gathering restrictions and accelerating retailer shutdowns effectively told investors that mall rent collection occupancy and liquidity were about to come under intense pressure.

primary_cause: No Southern-specific negative. Defensive utilities sold because investors began discounting lower commercial and industrial power demand. EIA later projected U.S. electricity consumption would fall record 4.6% in 2020
secondary_factors: Indiscriminate selling. Sensitivity to capital-market conditions
store_description: Utilities were not spared on March 16 because the market suddenly stopped treating them as safe havens and started pricing demand destruction from business closures. No Southern-specific negative catalyst in the prior 72 hours.
